title: More Forest Land May Not Fix Loggers' Biggest Problems
summary: President Trump is widely expected to soon open about 44 million acres of the country's last pristine national forests. He says this will bring timber jobs back to struggling small towns and help prevent wildfires in overgrown land. Last year, he signed actions to boost timber sales and reverse the Roadless Rule, which has blocked most new logging on undeveloped national forest land since 2001. But people who work in the forests say the problems are much bigger than getting more trees. Sean Smith, who runs Starfire Lumber in Cottage Grove, Oregon, says diesel fuel costs a record-high price, and steel, sawblades and other parts cost more too. Logger Jeff Brink says few people want to wake at 2 a.m. and drive a log truck for about the same pay as working at McDonald's. Experts say opening the forests may raise federal timber sales by only five to ten percent.
why_it_matters: Forests, jobs, and wildfire safety shape the towns where some children live and the wild places they may visit.

keywords.explanation: Pristine means untouched and in its natural, original state.
Timber is wood from trees that is cut for building and other uses.
The Roadless Rule is a rule that has blocked most new logging on undeveloped national forest land.
Sawblades are the sharp cutting parts of a saw.
Diesel is a kind of fuel used to run trucks and heavy machines.
An acre is a unit used to measure a piece of land.

background_read: National forests are large areas of forest land owned by the country, and logging means cutting trees there for wood.
A rule has blocked most new logging on undeveloped forest land, because roads and cutting change wild places.
Opening more land to logging could bring timber jobs to small towns, but workers say high fuel and equipment costs and a shortage of workers are bigger problems.
